sources.title: Great Basin People
sources.note: NPS synthesis of long occupation, marsh and upland resources, pinyon, fiber technology, shell exchange and archaeological change in the Great Basin.

sources.title: Historic Tribes of the Great Basin
sources.note: NPS account of distinct later Shoshone, Paiute, Ute and Washoe histories, family groups, seasonal rounds and varied subsistence, used only as labeled comparison.

sources.title: Fremont Culture
sources.note: NPS archaeological summary of localized Fremont basketry, footwear, figurines, pottery, villages, storage, cultivation, hunting and later transformation.

sources.title: Pine Nut Gathering
sources.note: NPS explanation of Great Basin pinyon harvests, nutritional value and continuing Indigenous gathering rights and knowledge.

sources.title: Nevada Caves: Hidden Cave
sources.note: BLM account of Hidden Cave excavation and evidence that artifact-rich cave deposits represent repeated caching rather than an ordinary house floor.

sources.title: Archaeology Collections
sources.note: Natural History Museum of Utah description of more than a million records and objects from Danger, Cowboy, Hogup and other sites and their research uses.

sources.title: Lovelock Cave Historic Site
sources.note: BLM site history, storage and shelter interpretation, excavation history and two-thousand-year-old tule duck decoys.

sources.title: Danger Cave Explorer Corps Marker
sources.note: Natural History Museum of Utah overview of Danger Cave layers, hearths, plant and animal remains, fiber, stone, ceramics and changing interpretations.

sources.title: Hidden Cave Junior Ranger
sources.note: BLM educational guide to Lake Lahontan marshes, cache use, artifacts, petroglyphs, archaeology and Fallon Paiute-Shoshone connections.

sources.title: Great Basin National Park General Management Plan
sources.note: NPS cultural-resource synthesis of Great Basin Archaic mobility, plant and animal foods, fiber, shell exchange and later seasonal rounds.

sources.title: Trees and Shrubs of Great Basin National Park
sources.note: NPS ecology and ethnobotany of pinyon, willow and other plants, used cautiously as later comparative knowledge rather than a target-wide medicine list.

sources.title: Baker Archeological Site Walking Tour
sources.note: NPS Fremont-village interpretation and explicit warning that archaeological material categories do not reveal a people’s language or full beliefs.

sources.title: Mojave National Preserve History and Culture
sources.note: NPS overview of distinct Mojave Desert histories, trails and later Chemehuevi plant gathering, hunting and exchange.

sources.title: Mojave National Preserve Water Resources Management Plan
sources.note: NPS management synthesis of springs, settlement constraints, archaeological water features and distinct later Chemehuevi and Mojave adaptations.

sources.title: Springs and Seeps of Mojave National Preserve
sources.note: NPS ecological account of groundwater, springs and seeps as scarce natural water across a vast desert landscape.

sources.title: Organ Pipe Cactus
sources.note: NPS account of cactus ecology and named O’odham fruit harvesting, processing and seasonal observance, used as later localized comparison.

sources.title: History and Culture at Organ Pipe Cactus
sources.note: NPS archaeological overview of long Sonoran Desert occupation, trails, shell, points, pottery, rock markings, agriculture and colonial arrival.

sources.title: O’odham
sources.note: NPS account of distinct later Desert and River O’odham settlement, water management and food production, used only as named comparison.

sources.title: Piute Creek
sources.note: NPS place history of a rare perennial stream, long Indigenous use, plant cultivation, travel, trade and later military intrusion.

sources.title: Mojave Culture
sources.note: Fort Mojave Tribal content hosted by NPS on named Mojave river farming, fishing, mesquite, trade, pottery, children, clans, dreams and ceremony.

sources.title: Mojave Tribe: Late History
sources.note: Fort Mojave Tribal account hosted by NPS of later reservation pressure, compulsory boarding school, punishment and cultural survival.

sources.title: Mojave Tribe: Early History
sources.note: Fort Mojave Tribal account hosted by NPS of later Spanish and American encounters, conflict and Mojave continuity after the card interval.

sources.title: Upper Pictograph Cave
sources.note: NPS description of localized Fremont pictographs, excavation evidence and the danger of inventing meanings for undeciphered images.

sources.title: Duck Decoys from Lovelock Cave
sources.note: National Museum of the American Indian catalog and Native knowledge-keeper interpretation of dated tule, feather, cordage and painted waterfowl decoys.

sources.title: Big Bend’s First Inhabitants
sources.note: NPS regional archaeology of Chihuahuan Desert climate, Archaic plant dependence, atlatls, later bows, pottery, cultivation and exchange.

sources.title: Archaeology in Big Bend
sources.note: NPS explanation of controlled excavation and analysis of pollen, charcoal, feces, stone debris, artifacts, diet and technology.

sources.title: Paleohydrology of Desert Wetlands
sources.note: USGS research on ancient springs, wetlands, groundwater change and animal corridors across Great Basin, Mojave, Sonoran and Chihuahuan deserts.

sources.title: The what, how and why of archaeological coprolite analysis
sources.note: Peer-reviewed review of desiccated feces research, preservation, diet and parasite evidence with Great Basin and Southwest case histories.

sources.title: Prehistoric Economy and Settlement in the Lower Pecos
sources.note: NPS-hosted scholarly synthesis of Lower Pecos plant foods, earth ovens, open camps, rockshelters, middens, quarries and rock-marking sites.

sources.title: Recovering parasites from mummies and coprolites
sources.note: Peer-reviewed review of archaeological parasite research showing strong variation through time, ecology, housing and subsistence in the Great Basin and Southwest.

proposedOverrides.summary: Broad western North American atlas umbrella for many desert and Great Basin societies; never one people, language, economy or polity.

batchIdentityNotes: Coordinates establish a western North American footprint spanning the Great Basin, California deserts, Southwest, Texas margins and northern Mexico; other-continent readings are rejected.
The exact indexed display name is “Desert hunter-gatherers,” but the record is a broad imported atlas umbrella, not a self-named people, language, state, uniform economy or archaeological culture.
The opening feature combines marsh, mountain, river, cactus and dry-basin environments plus mobile foraging, caching, village life, farming and mixed economies.

At 800 CE the geometry abruptly contracts from one huge polygon to Great Basin remnants while overbroad Anasazi and Mogollon layers absorb distant tested points; this is treated as an editorial taxonomy cut.
The target is absent at 1492, returns as one Great Basin polygon at 1500 and is absent at 1530. These gaps are not population disappearance or a successor chain.
Named archaeological patterns and living nations remain distinct. Later ethnography appears only as explicit localized comparison.
No built target-wide toilet, medicine system, family rule, gender division, army, religion, school or political system is invented.
Contemporaneous written-language sample: none is securely attributable. Rock markings are not recast as a deciphered umbrella script, and no neighboring language is borrowed.
